Two things count.
Midterm (25%): a report to a Board built on the study of a cost, a revenue and a profit function. Due 1 Nov.
Final exam (75%): 3 hours, paper, calculator. One of five questions is pure calculus: integrals, limits, recovering a function from its derivative.

Every technique in this room is here because one of those two asks for it. I will tell you which one, every time.

title: Revision of mathematics, told as business decisions
section: The shape of an exam item
text:
The shape of an exam item


Same form as the final, different numbers:
\int \frac{x^{5} - 3x^{3} + 2}{x^{2}}\,dx \lim_{x \to 1^{+}} \frac{(x-1)^{2}}{x - x^{2}} f'(x) = 6x^{2} - 2x,\quad f(1) = 4 \;\Rightarrow\; f(x) = ?

Today we do none of this. Today we make sure that when we get there, the algebra underneath — dividing term by term, factoring, solving for an unknown, handling a log — is not what slows you down.
Everything today is a question the founder of a small firm actually has to answer.

The case: Arno Bikes



e-bike assembler, Florence



Fixed cost

Variable cost
€400 per bike (parts, packaging)


List price
€1,000 per bike



Four questions from the founder, one per block:
A. How many bikes before I stop losing money? · B. How many bikes should I make? C. How long until revenue doubles? · D. Is this battery cell within spec?

title: Revision of mathematics, told as business decisions
section: How many bikes a month before Arno Bikes stops losing money?
text:
How many bikes a month before Arno Bikes stops losing money?







Bet before we compute


Write a number. Do not compute yet.




Two facts, written as two functions of the monthly quantity q:
C(q) = 60{,}000 + 400\,q \qquad\qquad R(q) = 1{,}000\,q

Break-even is where they meet: R(q) = C(q).

title: Revision of mathematics, told as business decisions
section: Two lines and a crossing
text:
Two lines and a crossing




1{,}000\,q = 60{,}000 + 400\,q 600\,q = 60{,}000 q^{*} = \frac{60{,}000}{600} = 100
Reading. €600 is the contribution of each bike. Break-even is fixed cost ÷ contribution.

title: Revision of mathematics, told as business decisions
section: Move the price. Then raise the rent.
text:
Move the price. Then raise the rent.
LAB · session.ipynb § A

Bet: what price makes break-even 50 bikes? Then slide.
The landlord raises fixed cost to €72,000. Before running: what happens to the cost line, and to the crossing?

Watch the slope and the intercept separately. Only one of them moved.

title: Revision of mathematics, told as business decisions
section: A cost shock is a parallel shift — remember this for the midterm
text:
A cost shock is a parallel shift — remember this for the midterm




Same slope (€400 per bike), higher intercept.
New break-even: 1{,}000q = 72{,}000 + 400q \Rightarrow q^{*} = 120.
The midterm asks how a tariff on an input changes the cost and profit schedules. That is this picture with different names: a per-unit tariff changes the slope, a lump-sum cost changes the intercept.

title: Revision of mathematics, told as business decisions
section: The whole market: two facts, two unknowns
text:
The whole market: two facts, two unknowns
Buyers in Tuscany: Q_d = 1200 - 2p. Sellers: Q_s = -300 + 3p.







Bet before we compute


What price clears the market?






Substitution 1200 - 2p = -300 + 3p 1500 = 5p p^{*} = 300, Q^{*} = 600

Elimination Q + 2p = 1200 Q - 3p = -300 subtract: 5p = 1500

Picture 








Board sentence


One equation is one fact about the business. Two unknowns need two facts. Write the facts as equations before touching a number.

section: Price responds to volume
text:
Price responds to volume
The founder learns: at €1,000 she sells 150 bikes; every €4 cut sells one more.
p(q) = 1600 - 4q
Revenue is price × quantity: a rectangle whose sides pull in opposite directions.







Bet before we compute


Does selling more always bring more revenue? Yes / no, and roughly where it stops.

title: Revision of mathematics, told as business decisions
section: Revenue, cost, profit
text:
Revenue, cost, profit
R(q) = (1600 - 4q)\,q = 1600q - 4q^{2} \pi(q) = R(q) - C(q) = -4q^{2} + 1200q - 60{,}000

Where is profit zero? First move, always: divide out the common factor.
q^{2} - 300q + 15{,}000 = 0 q = \frac{300 \pm \sqrt{300^{2} - 4\cdot 15{,}000}}{2} = \frac{300 \pm \sqrt{30{,}000}}{2} \approx 63.4,\;\; 236.6

title: Revision of mathematics, told as business decisions
section: The discriminant decides before you compute
text:
The discriminant decides before you compute





b^{2} - 4ac
roots
in business




> 0
two
a profitable window


= 0
one
a single break-even


< 0
none
no viable scale



Where is profit positive? A downward parabola (a<0) is positive between its roots:
63.4 < q < 236.6


The sign line. In the midterm it is called “the sign of the profit function”.

section: Push the fixed cost up. Where do the two break-evens merge?
text:
Push the fixed cost up. Where do the two break-evens merge?
LAB · session.ipynb § B

Bet on the fixed cost at which the roots become one. (Hint: what is the profit at the vertex now?)
Then push further. What does “no roots” look like, and what does it mean for the founder?

title: Revision of mathematics, told as business decisions
section: The top of the hill, for now
text:
The top of the hill, for now
Vertex of \pi(q) = -4q^{2} + 1200q - 60{,}000:
q_{v} = -\frac{b}{2a} = -\frac{1200}{-8} = 150 \qquad \pi(150) = 30{,}000
This formula works for parabolas only.
Next week you get a tool that finds the top of the hill for any curve — a log revenue, a cubic cost, anything. It is called the derivative, and it is the reason this course exists.







Board sentence


A quadratic has two roots, one, or none, and the discriminant tells you which before you compute. In business: a profitable window, a single break-even, no viable scale.

section: Revenue €1.2M, growing 12% a year
text:
Revenue €1.2M, growing 12% a year
R(t) = 1.2 \cdot 1.12^{\,t}
Linear growth adds the same amount each year. Exponential growth adds the same percentage.







Bet before we compute


How many years to double? Write a number.

title: Revision of mathematics, told as business decisions
section: Linear versus exponential growth
text:
Linear versus exponential growth



Clip rendered with manim from anim/src/week01_scenes.py.

title: Revision of mathematics, told as business decisions
section: The unknown is in the exponent
text:
The unknown is in the exponent
1.2 \cdot 1.12^{\,t} = 2.4 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 1.12^{\,t} = 2
No algebra so far reaches t. That is what a logarithm is for: it answers “to what power?”

\ln\!\left(1.12^{\,t}\right) = \ln 2 \;\Longrightarrow\; t\,\ln 1.12 = \ln 2 \;\Longrightarrow\; t = \frac{0.6931}{0.1133} \approx 6.1 \text{ years}









rule
reading




\ln(ab) = \ln a + \ln b
growth factors multiply, their logs add


\ln(a/b) = \ln a - \ln b
a ratio of revenues becomes a difference


\ln a^{k} = k \ln a
k years of the same growth: the exponent comes down


\log_{b} x = \ln x / \ln b
any base through the calculator’s \ln

title: Revision of mathematics, told as business decisions
section: The sanity check you will use in the exam
text:
The sanity check you will use in the exam
t_{\text{double}} \approx \frac{70}{g_{\%}} \qquad\qquad \frac{70}{12} \approx 5.8
Why it works: \ln 2 \approx 0.69 and \ln(1+g) \approx g when g is small, so t = \ln 2 / \ln(1+g) \approx 0.69/g.
The number e \approx 2.718 appears today only as “the base your calculator’s \ln uses”. In week 4 it becomes continuous compounding and earns its place.







Board sentence


Whenever the unknown is in the exponent, take logs of both sides. Whenever you see a log, remember it is a question: to what power?

title: Revision of mathematics, told as business decisions
section: Is this cell within spec?
text:
Is this cell within spec?
Battery cells must be 500\,\text{Wh} \pm 15. A supplier ships one at 483 Wh.







Bet before we compute


In or out? Then write the rule as one inequality.





|c - 500| \le 15 \;\Longleftrightarrow\; 485 \le c \le 515 \;\Longleftrightarrow\; c \in [485,\,515]





|x-a| is the distance from a. “\le b” is the closed interval [a-b,\,a+b]; “> b” is the two tails x<a-b or x>a+b. Square bracket: endpoint included. Round bracket: excluded, or \pm\infty. The exam asks for domains written exactly like this.

Sixty seconds to the Board
One of you stands up. The other is the Board.
Tell them, with numbers and no formulas:

where Arno Bikes breaks even at today’s price;
between which volumes it makes money once price responds to volume, and how fragile that window is;

The Board asks one question. This is a rehearsal of the midterm’s oral.

Slides are the spine of each session: an HTML deck with the clips embedded (arrow keys to move, F for full screen), plus a PDF for printing. Notebook is what you see on the projector: open it in Colab if you want to move the sliders yourself, nothing to install. Drills are the paper exercises we do in class, in exam format, with worked solutions at the bottom. Clips are the short animations shown in class.




How the five weeks work the contract, stated once


Every technique serves an exam item. Weeks 1–3 build the study of a function by hand for the midterm and Q5 of the final. Weeks 4–5 build the financial mathematics the exam and the resit ask for. You are told, each time, which one.
Decision → picture → technique → decision. Each block opens with a business question, shows the picture on screen, then does the technique on paper, and closes with one sentence you could say to a Board.
Half slides, half laboratory. About forty minutes of slides and notebook, eighty minutes of guided hand computation, a Board pitch by one student, ten minutes of homework briefing. Real break mid-session.
Weekly rhythm. Thursday lesson. Drill solutions and homework online by Friday. Homework due Wednesday 23:59 on Moodle, as a photo or PDF of your paper. The first fifteen minutes of the next session are the walkthrough: one student explains one drill at the board.
Homework is formative. It is not graded, but it is read, discussed, and it is part of the evidence used when the midterm is marked.
Running case: Arno Bikes, an e-bike assembler in Florence. Fixed cost €60,000 a month, variable cost €400 a bike, list price €1,000, demand p = 1600 − 4q. Every drill reuses its shape with different numbers, so that by week 3 the midterm case is a familiar object.


Assessment module scheme, set by ESE


Midterm assignment — 25%. A 1,500-word research paper (±10%) plus an 8–15 minute oral presentation. Written part 80%, oral 20%. Guidelines are briefed in class in week 2 and published on the student portal. Paper due Sunday 1 November, 23:59 on Turnitin; orals in the week of 2 November, on the day set by the module leader. No late submission for postgraduate work; a failed or missing submission gives one in-term resubmission capped at 50%.
Final examination — 75%. Three hours in class, five questions of equal weight, all work shown, non-programmable calculator only, no notes. Weeks 1–5 train you for the pure calculus question (limits, derivatives, integrals of rational functions with log terms) and the financial-mathematics items.
Reassessment. Re-sit examination, 100%, capped at 40% by ESE regulation.

title: Week 1 — Drills
text:
Exam format. Show all work. Core items are for everyone; stretch items for whoever finishes early. Solutions at the end, worked the way an examiner wants to see them.


D1 (core). Arno Bikes has fixed monthly costs of €60,000 and a variable cost of €400 per bike. Bikes sell at €1,000. (a) Write the cost function C(q) and the revenue function R(q). (b) Find the break-even quantity. (c) The landlord raises the rent so that fixed costs become €72,000. Find the new break-even quantity and state in one sentence what happened to the cost line in the (q, €) plane.
D2 (core). In the Tuscan e-bike market, demand is Q_d = 1200 − 2p and supply is Q_s = −300 + 3p (p in €, Q in bikes per month). (a) Find the equilibrium price and quantity. (b) The region introduces a tax of €50 per bike paid by sellers, so that sellers now respond to the price they keep, p − 50. Write the new supply function and find the new equilibrium. (c) How much of the €50 tax is paid by buyers, in the form of a higher price?
D3 (stretch). A workshop assembles two models. Model A takes 2 hours, model B takes 3 hours; 1,200 hours are available per month and the plan is 500 bikes in total. Set up and solve the system giving the number of each model.



D4 (core). A firm’s profit function is π(q) = −2q² + 600q − 40,000. (a) Find the quantities at which profit is zero. (b) For which quantities is the firm profitable? (c) Find the vertex of the parabola and interpret it.
D5 (core). Solve the inequalities: (a) x² − 7x + 10 ≤ 0 (b) 2x² + 3x − 2 > 0
D6 (stretch — the final-exam pattern). Factor numerator and denominator, then simplify: (x − 1)² / (x − x²). Evaluate the simplified expression at x = 1.1 and at x = 0.9 and comment on the sign.



D7 (core). (a) Simplify: ln(e³), log₂ 32, ln(a²b / c). (b) Solve for x: 3ˣ = 81; 10ˣ = 500 (three decimals).
D8 (core). Arno Bikes’ revenue is €1.2M and grows at 12% a year. (a) Write revenue after t years. (b) How many years to double? Check with the rule of 70. (c) How many years to reach €3M?
D9 (stretch). (a) Solve 5e^{0.03t} = 8 for t. (b) A competitor doubled revenue in 5 years. What constant annual growth rate does that imply?



D10 (core). (a) Battery cells must be 500 Wh ± 15 Wh. Write the condition with an absolute value and as an interval. Is a 483 Wh cell acceptable? (b) Solve |x − 3| > 2.
D11 (core — notation for the exam). Write as intervals: (a) x ≥ −3; (b) x > −3; (c) −3 < x ≤ 5. Then state the domain, as an interval, of (d) f(x) = √(x + 3) and (e) g(x) = ln(x − 1).



Solutions

D1. (a) C(q) = 60,000 + 400q; R(q) = 1,000q. (b) R = C → 1,000q = 60,000 + 400q → 600q = 60,000 → q = 100 bikes. (Contribution per bike €600; 60,000 / 600 = 100.) (c) 1,000q = 72,000 + 400q → q = 120. The cost line shifted up in parallel by €12,000 (same slope, higher intercept); the crossing with the revenue line moved right.
D2. (a) 1200 − 2p = −300 + 3p → 1500 = 5p → p = €300; Q = 1200 − 600 = 600. (b) Q_s = −300 + 3(p − 50) = −450 + 3p. Then 1200 − 2p = −450 + 3p → 1650 = 5p → p = €330, Q = 540. (c) Buyers pay €330 instead of €300: €30 of the €50 is passed to buyers; sellers keep 330 − 50 = 280, i.e. bear €20.
D3. Let x = model A, y = model B. 2x + 3y = 1200, x + y = 500. From the second, x = 500 − y; substitute: 1000 − 2y + 3y = 1200 → y = 200, x = 300. 300 of A, 200 of B.
D4. (a) Divide by −2: q² − 300q + 20,000 = 0. Discriminant 300² − 4·20,000 = 90,000 − 80,000 = 10,000, √ = 100. q = (300 ± 100)/2 → q = 100 and q = 200. (b) Downward parabola (a = −2 < 0) is positive between its roots: 100 < q < 200. (c) Vertex at q = −b/(2a) = −600/(−4) = 150; π(150) = −2·22,500 + 90,000 − 40,000 = **€5,000**. Maximum profit is €5,000 at 150 units; the window is narrow, the business is fragile.
D5. (a) Roots of x² − 7x + 10: (x − 2)(x − 5) → 2 and 5. Upward parabola ≤ 0 between roots: 2 ≤ x ≤ 5, i.e. [2, 5]. (b) Roots: x = (−3 ± √(9 + 16))/4 = (−3 ± 5)/4 → x = 1/2 and x = −2. Upward parabola > 0 outside the roots: x < −2 or x > 1/2.
D6. x − x² = x(1 − x) = −x(x − 1). So (x − 1)² / (−x(x − 1)) = −(x − 1)/x for x ≠ 0, 1. At x = 1.1: −0.1/1.1 ≈ −0.091. At x = 0.9: −(−0.1)/0.9 ≈ +0.111. The expression changes sign across x = 1 — approaching 1 from the right it is a small negative number, from the left a small positive number. (This is the algebra behind the one-sided limits the final exam asks for: factor, cancel, then look at the sign of what is left. The limit from the right is 0⁻.)
D7. (a) ln(e³) = 3; log₂ 32 = 5 (2⁵ = 32); ln(a²b/c) = 2 ln a + ln b − ln c. (b) 3ˣ = 81 = 3⁴ → x = 4. 10ˣ = 500 → x = log₁₀ 500 = **2.699**.
D8. (a) R(t) = 1.2 · 1.12ᵗ (€M). (b) 1.12ᵗ = 2 → t ln 1.12 = ln 2 → t = 0.6931 / 0.1133 = **6.1 years**. Rule of 70: 70/12 ≈ 5.8 — consistent. (c) 1.12ᵗ = 2.5 → t = ln 2.5 / ln 1.12 = 0.9163 / 0.1133 = **8.1 years**.
D9. (a) e^{0.03t} = 1.6 → 0.03t = ln 1.6 = 0.4700 → t ≈ 15.7. (b) (1 + g)⁵ = 2 → 1 + g = 2^{1/5} = e^{(ln 2)/5} = e^{0.1386} = 1.1487 → g ≈ 14.9% a year.
D10. (a) |c − 500| ≤ 15 ↔︎ 485 ≤ c ≤ 515, i.e. [485, 515]. 483 < 485: not acceptable. (b) |x − 3| > 2 ↔︎ x − 3 > 2 or x − 3 < −2 ↔︎ x > 5 or x < 1.
D11. (a) [−3, +∞); (b) (−3, +∞); (c) (−3, 5]. (d) Need x + 3 ≥ 0 → [−3, +∞). (e) Need x − 1 > 0 → (1, +∞). (Square bracket when the endpoint is included, round when it is not or when it is ±∞. The resit asks exactly this.)

D2. (a) 1200 − 2p = −300 + 3p → 1500 = 5p → p = €300; Q = 1200 − 600 = 600. (b) Q_s = −300 + 3(p − 50) = −450 + 3p. Then 1200 − 2p = −450 + 3p → 1650 = 5p → p = €330, Q = 540. (c) Buyers pay €330 instead of €300: €30 of the €50 is passed to buyers; sellers keep 330 − 50 = 280, i.e. bear €20.
D3. Let x = model A, y = model B. 2x + 3y = 1200, x + y = 500. From the second, x = 500 − y; substitute: 1000 − 2y + 3y = 1200 → y = 200, x = 300. 300 of A, 200 of B.
D4. (a) Divide by −2: q² − 300q + 20,000 = 0. Discriminant 300² − 4·20,000 = 90,000 − 80,000 = 10,000, √ = 100. q = (300 ± 100)/2 → q = 100 and q = 200. (b) Downward parabola (a = −2 < 0) is positive between its roots: 100 < q < 200. (c) Vertex at q = −b/(2a) = −600/(−4) = 150; π(150) = −2·22,500 + 90,000 − 40,000 = **€5,000**. Maximum profit is €5,000 at 150 units; the window is narrow, the business is fragile.
D5. (a) Roots of x² − 7x + 10: (x − 2)(x − 5) → 2 and 5. Upward parabola ≤ 0 between roots: 2 ≤ x ≤ 5, i.e. [2, 5]. (b) Roots: x = (−3 ± √(9 + 16))/4 = (−3 ± 5)/4 → x = 1/2 and x = −2. Upward parabola > 0 outside the roots: x < −2 or x > 1/2.
D6. x − x² = x(1 − x) = −x(x − 1). So (x − 1)² / (−x(x − 1)) = −(x − 1)/x for x ≠ 0, 1. At x = 1.1: −0.1/1.1 ≈ −0.091. At x = 0.9: −(−0.1)/0.9 ≈ +0.111. The expression changes sign across x = 1 — approaching 1 from the right it is a small negative number, from the left a small positive number. (This is the algebra behind the one-sided limits the final exam asks for: factor, cancel, then look at the sign of what is left. The limit from the right is 0⁻.)
D7. (a) ln(e³) = 3; log₂ 32 = 5 (2⁵ = 32); ln(a²b/c) = 2 ln a + ln b − ln c. (b) 3ˣ = 81 = 3⁴ → x = 4. 10ˣ = 500 → x = log₁₀ 500 = **2.699**.
D8. (a) R(t) = 1.2 · 1.12ᵗ (€M). (b) 1.12ᵗ = 2 → t ln 1.12 = ln 2 → t = 0.6931 / 0.1133 = **6.1 years**. Rule of 70: 70/12 ≈ 5.8 — consistent. (c) 1.12ᵗ = 2.5 → t = ln 2.5 / ln 1.12 = 0.9163 / 0.1133 = **8.1 years**.
D9. (a) e^{0.03t} = 1.6 → 0.03t = ln 1.6 = 0.4700 → t ≈ 15.7. (b) (1 + g)⁵ = 2 → 1 + g = 2^{1/5} = e^{(ln 2)/5} = e^{0.1386} = 1.1487 → g ≈ 14.9% a year.
D10. (a) |c − 500| ≤ 15 ↔︎ 485 ≤ c ≤ 515, i.e. [485, 515]. 483 < 485: not acceptable. (b) |x − 3| > 2 ↔︎ x − 3 > 2 or x − 3 < −2 ↔︎ x > 5 or x < 1.
D11. (a) [−3, +∞); (b) (−3, +∞); (c) (−3, 5]. (d) Need x + 3 ≥ 0 → [−3, +∞). (e) Need x − 1 > 0 → (1, +∞). (Square bracket when the endpoint is included, round when it is not or when it is ±∞. The resit asks exactly this.)

title: Homework 1 — due Wednesday 30 September, 23:59 (Moodle)
text:
Two parts. Part 1 is done on paper and handed in as a photo or scan; Part 2 is a short typed text. Expect 2–3 hours in total. Both parts are formative: they are not graded, but they are read, they are discussed in the first 15 minutes of next session, and they are part of the evidence I use when I mark your midterm.


H1. A café has fixed costs of €9,000 a month. Each coffee sells for €2.50 and costs €0.70 to make. (a) Break-even in coffees per month. (b) The owner wants a profit of €3,000 a month. How many coffees? (c) The price is cut to €2.20 to fight a competitor. New break-even, and the sentence you would tell the owner.
H2. Demand: Q_d = 900 − 3p. Supply: Q_s = −100 + 2p. (a) Equilibrium price and quantity. (b) A subsidy of €25 per unit is paid to sellers (they respond to p + 25). New equilibrium. (c) Sketch both situations on one graph: axes labelled, both lines, both equilibria marked.
H3. A firm’s profit is π(q) = −q² + 80q − 1,200. (a) Quantities with zero profit. (b) The profitable range, written as an interval. (c) The quantity that maximises profit and the maximum profit. (d) For which fixed cost (replace the 1,200) would the firm have exactly one break-even point?
H4. Solve: (a) x² − 9 > 0; (b) −x² + 4x − 3 ≥ 0. Write each answer as an interval or union of intervals.
H5. Factor and simplify (x − 3)² / (3x − x²). Evaluate at x = 3.01 and x = 2.99. What is the sign on each side of 3?
H6. A subscription business has 4,000 subscribers growing 6% a month. (a) Subscribers after t months (formula) and after 12 months (number). (b) Months to reach 10,000. (c) Months to double, exactly and with the rule of 70.
H7. Solve for t: (a) 200 · 1.05ᵗ = 350; (b) e^{0.08t} = 3.
H8. (a) Solve |x − 12| ≤ 4 and |2x − 1| > 5. (b) Give the domain, as an interval, of f(x) = ln(2x − 6) and of g(x) = √(10 − x).

title: MBA03 · Week 1 — Revision of mathematics, told as business decisions
text:
European School of Economics · Thu 24 Sep 2026 · Tutor: Niccolò Salvini
Running case: Arno Bikes, e-bike assembler in Florence. Fixed cost €60,000 / month · variable cost €400 / bike · list price €1,000.
This notebook is driven by the tutor. Every picture here is followed by the same computation by hand on paper — that is what the exam asks for.
# Setup (Colab has plotly and sympy preinstalled; this is a no-op there)
import subprocess, sys
try:
    import plotly, sympy
except ImportError:
    subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "install", "-q", "plotly", "sympy"])
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
import sympy as sp
np.set_printoptions(precision=3, suppress=True)
print("ready")

title: MBA03 · Week 1 — Revision of mathematics, told as business decisions
section: A. Launch or not? — break-even and equilibrium
text:
A. Launch or not? — break-even and equilibrium
Question for the Board: how many bikes a month before Arno Bikes stops losing money?
\[C(q) = 60{,}000 + 400\,q \qquad R(q) = 1{,}000\,q\]
Break-even is the quantity where the two lines cross: \(R(q) = C(q)\).
Business reading: every bike contributes €600 (price minus variable cost); break-even is fixed cost ÷ contribution.

FIXED, VC = 60_000, 400
q = np.linspace(0, 300, 301)

def breakeven_fig(prices=(700, 800, 900, 1000, 1200, 1400, 1600), fixed=FIXED):
    fig = go.Figure()
    frames = []
    for p in prices:
        be = fixed / (p - VC)
        frames.append(go.Frame(
            name=str(p),
            data=[go.Scatter(x=q, y=fixed + VC*q, name="Cost C(q)", line=dict(color="#c0392b", width=3)),
                  go.Scatter(x=q, y=p*q, name=f"Revenue R(q), p = €{p}", line=dict(color="#2471a3", width=3)),
                  go.Scatter(x=[be], y=[p*be], mode="markers+text", text=[f"break-even ≈ {be:.0f}"],
                             textposition="top left", marker=dict(size=12, color="black"), name="break-even")]))
    fig.add_traces(frames[3].data)
    fig.frames = frames
    fig.update_layout(
        title="Break-even: where revenue crosses cost",
        xaxis_title="bikes per month (q)", yaxis_title="€ per month", yaxis_range=[0, 300_000],
        sliders=[dict(active=3, currentvalue=dict(prefix="price €"),
                      steps=[dict(method="animate", label=f.name,
                                  args=[[f.name], dict(mode="immediate", frame=dict(duration=0, redraw=True))]) for f in frames])],
        template="plotly_white", height=480)
    return fig

breakeven_fig().show()

Bet before sliding: what price makes break-even 50 bikes?
Then: the landlord raises the rent. Re-run the cell below and watch the cost line — same slope, higher intercept, crossing moves right. This is exactly the mechanism behind the midterm’s Q4 (a tariff shifts the cost schedule).

breakeven_fig(fixed=72_000).show()


Market equilibrium — two facts, two unknowns
\[Q_d = 1200 - 2p \qquad Q_s = -300 + 3p\]
Setting \(Q_d = Q_s\): \(\;1500 = 5p \Rightarrow p^* = 300,\; Q^* = 600\).
The algebra is the answer; the picture is the check.

p = np.linspace(0, 600, 601)
Qd, Qs = 1200 - 2*p, -300 + 3*p
fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_scatter(x=Qd, y=p, name="Demand  Q = 1200 − 2p", line=dict(color="#2471a3", width=3))
fig.add_scatter(x=Qs, y=p, name="Supply  Q = −300 + 3p", line=dict(color="#c0392b", width=3))
fig.add_scatter(x=[600], y=[300], mode="markers+text", text=["(600, €300)"], textposition="middle right",
                marker=dict(size=12, color="black"), name="equilibrium")
fig.update_layout(title="Equilibrium (economists put price on the vertical axis)",
                  xaxis_title="bikes per month (Q)", yaxis_title="price (€)",
                  xaxis_range=[0, 1300], yaxis_range=[0, 600], template="plotly_white", height=450)
fig.show()

title: MBA03 · Week 1 — Revision of mathematics, told as business decisions
section: B. How many bikes? — quadratics
text:
B. How many bikes? — quadratics
Price now responds to volume: \(p(q) = 1600 - 4q\). Revenue is price × quantity, a rectangle whose sides pull in opposite directions:
\[R(q) = (1600 - 4q)\,q = 1600q - 4q^2\]
\[\pi(q) = R(q) - C(q) = -4q^2 + 1200q - 60{,}000\]
Bet: does selling more always bring more revenue?

qq = np.linspace(0, 400, 401)
R = (1600 - 4*qq) * qq
fig = go.Figure()
frames = []
for q0 in range(0, 401, 25):
    p0 = 1600 - 4*q0
    frames.append(go.Frame(name=str(q0), data=[
        go.Scatter(x=qq, y=1600 - 4*qq, name="demand p(q)", line=dict(color="#7f8c8d", dash="dot"), yaxis="y2"),
        go.Scatter(x=[0, q0, q0, 0, 0], y=[0, 0, p0, p0, 0], fill="toself", fillcolor="rgba(36,113,163,0.25)",
                   line=dict(color="#2471a3"), name=f"rectangle p·q = {p0*q0:,.0f}", yaxis="y2"),
        go.Scatter(x=qq[qq <= q0], y=R[qq <= q0], name="revenue R(q)", line=dict(color="#2471a3", width=3)),
        go.Scatter(x=[q0], y=[p0*q0], mode="markers", marker=dict(size=10, color="black"), showlegend=False)]))
fig.add_traces(frames[6].data); fig.frames = frames
fig.update_layout(
    title="Revenue is the area of the rectangle price × quantity",
    xaxis_title="bikes (q)", yaxis=dict(title="revenue €", range=[0, 170_000]),
    yaxis2=dict(title="price €", overlaying="y", side="right", range=[0, 1700]),
    sliders=[dict(active=6, currentvalue=dict(prefix="q = "),
                  steps=[dict(method="animate", label=f.name,
                              args=[[f.name], dict(mode="immediate", frame=dict(duration=0, redraw=True))]) for f in frames])],
    template="plotly_white", height=500)
fig.show()


Where is profit zero? Where is it positive?
Divide by the common factor first: \(\;q^2 - 300q + 15{,}000 = 0\)
\[q = \frac{300 \pm \sqrt{300^2 - 4\cdot 15{,}000}}{2} = \frac{300 \pm \sqrt{30{,}000}}{2} \approx 63.4,\; 236.6\]
A downward parabola is positive between its roots: profitable for \(63.4 < q < 236.6\).
Bet before sliding: at what fixed cost do the two break-evens merge into one?

def profit_fig(fixed_values=(40_000, 50_000, 60_000, 70_000, 80_000, 90_000, 100_000)):
    qq = np.linspace(0, 320, 641)
    fig = go.Figure(); frames = []
    for F in fixed_values:
        pi = -4*qq**2 + 1200*qq - F
        disc = 300**2 - 4*(F/4)
        if disc > 0:
            r1, r2 = (300 - disc**0.5)/2, (300 + disc**0.5)/2
            label = f"roots {r1:.1f} and {r2:.1f} — profitable window"
        elif disc == 0:
            r1 = r2 = 150; label = "one root at 150 — single break-even"
        else:
            r1 = r2 = None; label = "no roots — no viable scale"
        data = [go.Scatter(x=qq, y=pi, name="profit π(q)", line=dict(color="#1e8449", width=3)),
                go.Scatter(x=qq, y=np.zeros_like(qq), name="zero", line=dict(color="black", width=1)),
                go.Scatter(x=[150], y=[-4*150**2 + 1200*150 - F], mode="markers+text", text=["vertex"],
                           textposition="top center", marker=dict(size=10, color="#1e8449"), name="vertex")]
        if r1 is not None:
            data.append(go.Scatter(x=[r1, r2], y=[0, 0], mode="markers", marker=dict(size=12, color="#c0392b"), name="roots"))
        frames.append(go.Frame(name=f"{F:,}", data=data, layout=go.Layout(title=f"Fixed cost €{F:,}: {label}")))
    fig.add_traces(frames[2].data); fig.frames = frames
    fig.update_layout(title=frames[2].layout.title, xaxis_title="bikes (q)", yaxis_title="profit €",
                      yaxis_range=[-60_000, 60_000],
                      sliders=[dict(active=2, currentvalue=dict(prefix="fixed cost €"),
                                    steps=[dict(method="animate", label=f.name,
                                                args=[[f.name], dict(mode="immediate", frame=dict(duration=0, redraw=True))]) for f in frames])],
                      template="plotly_white", height=480)
    return fig
profit_fig().show()

Vertex: \(q = -\dfrac{b}{2a} = 150\), \(\pi(150) = 30{,}000\). Week 2 gives a tool that finds this point for any curve, not only parabolas.

title: MBA03 · Week 1 — Revision of mathematics, told as business decisions
section: C. How long to double? — exponentials and logarithms
text:
C. How long to double? — exponentials and logarithms
Revenue €1.2M growing 12% a year: \(\;R(t) = 1.2 \cdot 1.12^{\,t}\).
Linear growth adds the same amount each year; exponential growth adds the same percentage.
Bet: how many years to double?

t = np.linspace(0, 12, 241)
lin = 1.2 + 0.144*t          # +12% of the *initial* revenue every year
expo = 1.2 * 1.12**t
t_double = np.log(2)/np.log(1.12)
fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_scatter(x=t, y=lin, name="linear: +€144k a year", line=dict(color="#7f8c8d", width=3))
fig.add_scatter(x=t, y=expo, name="exponential: ×1.12 a year", line=dict(color="#2471a3", width=3))
fig.add_hline(y=2.4, line=dict(color="black", dash="dash"), annotation_text="double (€2.4M)")
fig.add_scatter(x=[t_double], y=[2.4], mode="markers+text", text=[f"{t_double:.1f} yrs"], textposition="bottom right",
                marker=dict(size=12, color="black"), showlegend=False)
fig.update_layout(title="Same start, same first-year gain, different futures",
                  xaxis_title="years", yaxis_title="revenue (€M)", template="plotly_white", height=450)
fig.show()
print(f"ln 2 / ln 1.12 = {np.log(2):.4f} / {np.log(1.12):.4f} = {t_double:.2f} years   (rule of 70: {70/12:.1f})")

The unknown is in the exponent. No algebra so far reaches it — that is what a logarithm is for:
\[1.12^{\,t} = 2 \;\Longrightarrow\; t \ln 1.12 = \ln 2 \;\Longrightarrow\; t = \frac{\ln 2}{\ln 1.12} \approx 6.1\]







rule
reading




\(\ln(ab) = \ln a + \ln b\)
growth factors multiply → their logs add


\(\ln(a/b) = \ln a - \ln b\)
a ratio of revenues becomes a difference


\(\ln a^{k} = k \ln a\)
\(k\) years of the same growth: the exponent comes down


\(\log_b x = \ln x / \ln b\)
any base through the calculator’s \(\ln\)



Rule of 70: \(t_{double} \approx 70/g_{\%}\), because \(\ln 2 \approx 0.69\) and \(\ln(1+g) \approx g\) for small \(g\).

# Growth-rate explorer: how sensitive is doubling time to g?
g = np.linspace(0.02, 0.30, 200)
fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_scatter(x=g*100, y=np.log(2)/np.log(1+g), name="exact  ln2 / ln(1+g)", line=dict(color="#2471a3", width=3))
fig.add_scatter(x=g*100, y=70/(g*100), name="rule of 70", line=dict(color="#c0392b", dash="dash", width=2))
fig.update_layout(title="Doubling time vs growth rate", xaxis_title="growth rate (% per year)",
                  yaxis_title="years to double", template="plotly_white", height=420)
fig.show()

title: MBA03 · Week 1 — Revision of mathematics, told as business decisions
section: D. Within tolerance — absolute value
text:
D. Within tolerance — absolute value
Battery cells must be 500 Wh ± 15 Wh:
\[|c - 500| \le 15 \;\Longleftrightarrow\; 485 \le c \le 515 \;\Longleftrightarrow\; c \in [485, 515]\]
\(|x-a|\) is the distance from \(a\). “≤ b” is the closed interval; “> b” is the two tails.

fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_scatter(x=[485, 515], y=[0, 0], mode="lines+markers", line=dict(color="#1e8449", width=8),
                marker=dict(size=14, symbol="line-ns-open"), name="|c − 500| ≤ 15")
fig.add_scatter(x=[500], y=[0], mode="markers+text", text=["500"], textposition="top center",
                marker=dict(size=10, color="black"), showlegend=False)
fig.add_scatter(x=[483], y=[0], mode="markers+text", text=["483 — rejected"], textposition="bottom center",
                marker=dict(size=12, color="#c0392b", symbol="x"), showlegend=False)
fig.update_layout(title="Tolerance band as an interval", xaxis_range=[470, 530], yaxis=dict(visible=False),
                  height=220, template="plotly_white", xaxis_title="Wh")
fig.show()

title: MBA03 · Week 1 — Revision of mathematics, told as business decisions
section: Tutor’s safety net — sympy checks of every drill answer
text:
Tutor’s safety net — sympy checks of every drill answer
(Collapsed in class. Run if a student’s answer disagrees with yours.)

x, q, p, t = sp.symbols('x q p t', real=True)
checks = {
 "D1b break-even": sp.solve(sp.Eq(1000*q, 60000 + 400*q), q),
 "D1c new break-even": sp.solve(sp.Eq(1000*q, 72000 + 400*q), q),
 "D2a equilibrium": sp.solve([sp.Eq(1200 - 2*p, -300 + 3*p)], p),
 "D2b with tax": sp.solve(sp.Eq(1200 - 2*p, -450 + 3*p), p),
 "D3 models": sp.solve([sp.Eq(2*x + 3*q, 1200), sp.Eq(x + q, 500)], [x, q]),
 "D4a roots": [sp.N(r, 4) for r in sp.solve(-2*q**2 + 600*q - 40000, q)],
 "D4c vertex": (150, -2*150**2 + 600*150 - 40000),
 "D5a": sp.solve_univariate_inequality(x**2 - 7*x + 10 <= 0, x),
 "D5b": sp.solve_univariate_inequality(2*x**2 + 3*x - 2 > 0, x),
 "D6 simplify": sp.simplify((x-2)**2 / (2*x - x**2)),
 "D7b 10^x=500": sp.N(sp.log(500, 10), 4),
 "D8b doubling": sp.N(sp.log(2)/sp.log(sp.Rational(112, 100)), 4),
 "D8c to 3M": sp.N(sp.log(sp.Rational(5, 2))/sp.log(sp.Rational(112, 100)), 4),
 "D9a": sp.N(sp.solve(sp.Eq(5*sp.exp(sp.Rational(3, 100)*t), 8), t)[0], 4),
 "D9b growth": sp.N(2**sp.Rational(1, 5) - 1, 4),
 "D10b": sp.solve_univariate_inequality(sp.Abs(x - 3) > 2, x),
 "Arno roots": [sp.N(r, 4) for r in sp.solve(-4*q**2 + 1200*q - 60000, q)],
}
for k, v in checks.items():
    print(f"{k:22s} → {v}")

title: How to work
text: Nothing is installed on your laptop and you are not asked to write code. The exam is on paper with a non-programmable calculator, so that is where the practice happens.

title: How to work
section: Bring to every session
text:
Bring to every session

Paper and pen. Drills are done by hand, in exam format, and kept: they are the record of your progress.
A non-programmable calculator. The same kind you will have in the final exam. Get used to it now: logs, powers, eˣ.
Renshaw, Maths for Economics (5th ed.), the module’s required text. Chapters per week are listed on the schedule.

title: How to work
section: Homework
text:
Homework
Set every Thursday, due Wednesday 23:59 on Moodle. Two parts, 2–3 hours in total:

A drill set on paper. Photograph or scan it and upload it as a single PDF. Show all work: the marks in the exam are for the method, and so is the feedback here.
A memo to the Board, 150–250 words, typed. Numbers and their meaning, no formulas in the text. This is a rehearsal of the register the midterm asks for.

Homework is formative: not graded, but read, discussed in the first fifteen minutes of the next session, and part of the evidence used when the midterm is marked.

title: How to work
section: The notebooks
text:
The notebooks
Each session has a Colab notebook driven by the tutor from the projector: sliders that move a parameter, the picture behind each formula, and a symbolic check of every drill’s answer. You can open it yourself from the Colab ↗ link on the schedule with any Google account; nothing to install, nothing to submit.

title: How to work
section: Drills and solutions
text:
Drills and solutions
The drills page of each week has the in-class exercises with worked solutions at the bottom, folded. Do the drill first, then open the solution and compare step by step, the way an examiner would.
Core items are for everyone. Stretch items are for whoever finishes early.

title: How to work
section: Writing mathematics the way the exam wants it
text:
Writing mathematics the way the exam wants it

Write the equation in words first (“break-even means revenue equals cost”), then in symbols.
Every quadratic: divide out the common factor, compute the discriminant, comment on its sign.
Every inequality: find the roots, draw the sign line, write the answer as an interval.
Every log problem: take logs of both sides, bring the exponent down, use the calculator only at the end.
Intervals: [ for included endpoints, ( for excluded ones and for ±∞.

title: How to work
section: Questions between sessions
text:
Questions between sessions
Use the course chat channel for quick questions and to arrange an office hour. Deliverables go on Moodle only.
